reads.title: Be passionate: what makes your heart sing?
reads.dek: Passion beats expertise on camera, and viewers can tell which one you've got.
reads.md:
Talk Like TED opens with one idea: if you're not passionate about what you're saying, why would the viewer care? Being an expert matters less than *showing* that you care. Viewers aren't stupid. They can tell.

The passion isn't about the product, though. You're not passionate about skincare. You're passionate about helping young guys improve their lives, and about entertaining them while you do it.

## The better question
"What are you passionate about?" is weak. Ask **"What makes my heart sing?"** Your answer, from your notes:

> Helping people improve the way they feel about themselves, so they can be themselves, express themselves however they like, and live happy in their teens and twenties. And entertaining them: seeing them react to what I made and like the way I made it.

## Why it works
- If the reason you make a video is money, it's hard to connect. If the reason is sharing your passion and improving someone's life, you connect.
- Emotions spread. A happy, charismatic person makes the people around him a bit happier, and a passionate one makes them a bit more passionate.
- Positive leaders persuade better than negative ones: to subscribe, to buy, or to eat more grilled cheese.
- Happiness creates success, not the other way round.

## For your future team
"When you are surrounded with people who share a collective passion around a common purpose, anything is possible." When you hire for the channel, use passion as a filter. Maybe the most important one.

checks.q: What's the stronger version of "what are you passionate about?"
checks.a: "What makes my heart sing?"

checks.q: What are you actually passionate about, if not skincare?
checks.a: Helping young guys feel better about themselves and live happier, while entertaining them.

reads.title: Storytelling: hero, villain and tiny emotions
reads.dek: Stories hit the heart first, then the head. On your channel they come in small doses every few seconds.
reads.md:
Aristotle said persuasion needs three things: **ethos** (credibility: what you've done, your experience), **logos** (logic, data, evidence) and **pathos** (emotion). Some of the most logical people alive agree you can't persuade with logic alone.

## Pathos on your channel
It isn't long, sad stories. It's small moments every few seconds:
- **Curiosity:** "There's one exception…"
- **Surprise:** "I expected this to work, but it didn't."
- **Humour**
- **Suspense:** "We'll come back to this."
- **Relief:** "The good news is…"

## Why stories work
- When someone tells a personal story, the listener's brain activity starts to sync with the teller's ("brain-to-brain coupling", Hasson's lab).
- Personal stories with an **unexpected result** stick best (Made to Stick).
- The simplest way to grab attention is to **break a pattern**. Curiosity is a gap in knowledge, and gaps feel uncomfortable. It should feel painful *not* to watch to the end.
- People want to see the human behind the product. That's why KFC has a face, why you like Icepro and Jawliner, and why AI-voice channels can't build a community.

## What a story is
Jonah Sachs (*Winning the Story Wars*): characters pursue a goal according to their values, face difficulty, and succeed or fail according to the storyteller's view of how the world works. Audiences have never been more sceptical, but when a story inspires them, they spread it for you.

## Hero, villain, townspeople
- **The hero** is your idea or method, or the viewer.
- **The villain** is a challenge, or the dark side of the community you stand against: blackpill, fake methods, people who hate the whole idea.
- **The townspeople** are your audience, who get saved from the villain and live happily ever after.

Give the audience at least one character to root for.

## Make it felt
When you describe things people can touch or smell, their sensory cortex responds. Use metaphors, analogies and vivid language. Avoid clichés and buzzwords: people tune out phrases they've heard a million times.

A line from your notes worth keeping: **"Improving your appearance is not about becoming worthy. It's about removing the barriers that stop you from expressing yourself."**

## The pitch test
Telling a story before asking for agreement works in real life too. Compare "Hey bro, I need an editor but can't pay you" with your BUas pitch: "you pay a university for four years to learn editing… or you learn it on a real channel, from someone who's done it, with real viewers giving feedback, for free, and if you stick with it, real money." Same ask, completely different result.

checks.q: The 3 parts of persuasion?
checks.a: Ethos (credibility), logos (logic and data), pathos (emotion).

checks.q: Who's the villain on your channel?
checks.a: Blackpill / extreme looksmaxxing, fake methods, the people who hate the whole idea.

reads.title: Have a conversation
reads.dek: Your note said "read this again". Practise until the script sounds like an exciting talk with a friend.
reads.md:
Talk Like TED's rule: **practise relentlessly and internalise the content, so you can deliver it as comfortably as a conversation with a close friend.** You flagged this as one of the most important things for your scripts, and it is.

## Why it works
Real persuasion happens after you've built an emotional connection and earned trust. If your voice, gestures and body language don't match your words, people stop trusting the message.

## What your first video taught you
It didn't sound like a conversation. The fix isn't "talk normally": it's an **exciting** conversation. Your voice needs to be higher and stronger than in real life for viewers to read it as normal. Still a conversation, never reading.

One speaker famous for perfect pace said he isn't reading to you, he's having a conversation with you, like a friend over dinner in a restaurant.

## For every line, ask
- Speed: fast here, or slow down?
- Volume and pitch: does it rise?
- Pauses: does this line need to breathe?
- Emphasis: which word carries it?

## Believe every line
If you don't believe what you're saying, your body or voice shows it. Short of being a trained FBI agent, you can't hide it. So never say anything you don't believe.

The way you dress, carry yourself and talk is how viewers decide whether to believe you. They've watched thousands of videos and can spot fake confidence too.

## Get real feedback
Ask lots of different people:
- What did you like most?
- What did you like least?
- What do you remember?

The book's three Ps: **Passion, Practice, Presence.**

checks.q: What should your delivery sound like?
checks.a: An exciting conversation with a friend: more energy than real life, never reading.

checks.q: The 3 feedback questions?
checks.a: What did you like most, what did you like least, what do you remember?

reads.title: Body language on camera
reads.dek: Gestures, posture and energy: what the camera reads before it hears a word.
reads.md:
## Gestures
People who think in complex ways use complex gestures. When someone is passionate, their hands move even if they try to stop them. The book's rules:
1. Use gestures. Let your hands be free.
2. Use them sparingly and naturally. Don't plan them; the story guides them.
3. Save your biggest gestures for the key moments.
4. Keep them above the waist, so eyes go to your face and hands.

Also: stand straight, make eye contact, and wear colours that pop against the background.

## Eager vs reserved
If you want to make an idea or offer more attractive, an **eager** style works better: animated, broad open movements, hands projected outward, leaning forward. The **reserved** style is the opposite: leaning back, small slow movements, slow speech.

Cut every mannerism that serves no purpose: clicking a pen, tapping fingers, spinning the chair. But don't freeze either. Move a bit.

## Before you film
Get your energy up: jump around, open your body up, move. You may have heard power posing raises testosterone. That part failed to replicate (Ranehill 2015), so don't say it on camera. Feeling a bit more confident is the honest version.

## A staging idea
One TED speaker with an injury put five chairs on stage. Each chair was one chapter of her story: the accident, ten days in hospital, and so on. She moved from chair to chair. Props can carry structure.

## Beyond the camera
Learning to command presence in real life (people listen to you, believe you, care what you say) is charisma and leadership practice. It helps the channel and it helps you get people to work with you.

checks.q: The 4 gesture rules?
checks.a: Hands free; sparingly and naturally; biggest at key moments; above the waist.

checks.q: Eager vs reserved style?
checks.a: Eager: animated, open, leaning forward (makes an offer attractive). Reserved: leaning back, small slow moves.

reads.title: Teach me something new
reads.dek: The brain is wired to notice what's new. Give it something it has never processed.
reads.md:
Spotting novelty is a survival tool every human shares. An unfamiliar or unexpected element grabs attention, breaks people's assumptions and gives them a new way of seeing the world.

Do one of three things:
- reveal information that's completely new to them,
- package familiar information in a new way,
- or offer a fresh way to solve an old problem.

## Your pattern interrupt
Your own idea: talk about blue and red, and let the viewer assume blue is the healthy choice. Then ask "so which one should you get?" and answer **red, because…**. The viewer was coasting, waiting for the answer he expected. The surprise snaps him back, makes him listen harder, and he remembers the moment.

## Why viewers watch
When you watch Rorz, you want one new thing you can *do*. That's the only reason. Teach your viewer something he can use in his daily life.

## Novelty and memory
New, surprising information gets remembered better: the brain marks it as worth keeping. The best teachers keep finding new ways to deliver the same material. Thumbnails show this cycle: a new style feels exciting, then everyone copies it and it stops working, then the next new style arrives.

## Package it
Hans Rosling made boring statistics unforgettable with moving country bubbles. How can your science be packaged visually?

Old communist blocks repainted in bright colours: same buildings, same people inside, completely different feeling. Repackage the *idea*, not only the title and thumbnail.

## Be a purple cow
A cow on the road is boring. A purple cow is amazing. A road full of purple cows is boring again. Aprilynne Alter's style is simple but remarkable. Put your own spin on things; don't just copy formats.

Study what works outside your niche too. A great persuader teaches you something even if he has no channel.

## Beginner's mind
Can you say the idea in one sentence? If someone asks a viewer "what was that guy talking about?", he should have one clear answer, and it should fit in a YouTube title.

Big picture before details. A caveman who meets a tiger doesn't ask how many teeth it has. He asks whether it'll eat him. Explain why we debloat before you explain potassium.

checks.q: Three ways to be novel?
checks.a: Brand-new information, a new package for known information, or a new way to solve an old problem.

checks.q: Why big picture first?
checks.a: People need the why before the how (the tiger: "will it eat me?" before "how many teeth?").

reads.title: Deliver a jaw-dropping moment
reads.dek: One scene everyone remembers. It takes 5% of the time and gets 100% of the memory.
reads.md:
Bill Gates gave a TED talk about malaria. He opened a jar of mosquitoes and said "there's no reason only poor people should have the experience." (He later said they weren't infected.) It was under 5% of his talk, and people still repeat it years later. Headlines wrote "Bill Gates releases mosquitoes on TED audience".

## Why it works
Psychologists call it an **emotionally charged event**. Shock, surprise, fear, sadness, joy and wonder all make memories stronger: the amygdala and stress hormones strengthen how the brain stores the moment. People *feel* they remember exactly where they were on 9/11, while they forget where they left their wallet this morning. (The 9/11 memories feel vivid but aren't perfectly accurate. The vividness is the point.)

## 5 ways to create one
1. **Props and demos**
2. **Unexpected, shocking statistics**
3. **Pictures, images and videos**
4. **Memorable headlines**: a short line people can repeat
5. **Personal stories**

## End on a high note
A showstopper. A singer ended her concert by zip-lining across the stadium. Put a moment at the end that brands the message into memory.

## How to find yours
Before scripting, know what the story is, what makes it interesting, what the format is and how it's packaged. Then list the most important points and ask: how can I make *this one* surprising?

Use several senses while planning: stand at a whiteboard, draw, think while walking. Anything that gets more of your brain involved.

## Importance makes memory
Higher perceived importance gets remembered more. You still watch Maurits's videos because you texted with him for one minute four years ago. A viewer you talk to personally in the Discord is far more likely to remember your videos five years from now.

checks.q: The 5 ways to create a jaw-dropping moment?
checks.a: Props/demos, shocking stats, pictures/video, a memorable repeatable line, personal stories.

checks.q: Why does an emotional moment stick?
checks.a: It's an emotionally charged event: emotion makes the brain store it more strongly.

reads.title: Lighten up: humour in your videos
reads.dek: The most-watched TED talk ever has one unusual thing: it's funny. Here's how to use humour without looking low-value.
reads.md:
The most popular TED talk of all time, Ken Robinson's "Do schools kill creativity?", has one thing most talks don't: humour. People love humour and they love novelty. Combine the two and you've got gold.

**Don't take yourself or your topic too seriously.**

## Why it works
- Humour lowers people's defences.
- It makes you likable, and people watch and buy from people they like.
- People with a good sense of humour get seen as friendlier, more considerate, more interesting, more intelligent and more emotionally stable.
- Laughter spreads positive feelings to others, which makes them like whoever is laughing.
- It reduces hostility, deflects criticism, relieves tension, lifts morale and helps deliver difficult messages.

Humour also ranks near the top of what people *say* they want in a partner. (Careful on camera: what people say they want and who they actually choose often differ, so don't claim it beats looks.)

## How to use it
- Make **humorous observations**, not jokes. Small and related to what you're saying.
- It must **amplify** the point (people more awake, more focused), never distract from it.
- Make yourself the joke. "I did something stupid" beats "my competitor did something stupid".
- Don't repeat stupid jokes. That backfires.
- It's a skill. Use it when it actually fits, creatively and naturally.
- Be authentic. Don't try to be someone you're not.
- If something made you laugh, it'll probably make others laugh too.

## 5 types
1. **Anecdotes and observations:** short stories that get a smile, not a big laugh.
2. **Analogies and metaphors:** compare two different things. Great for explaining something complex.
3. **Quotes:** funny ones, or ones you comment on in a funny way. Do your homework, and quotes from people you know count.
4. **Videos**
5. **Photos**

Balance humour, statistics and shock.

## For your channel
Facts on their own are unemotional, and humour packages them. Jokes like the banana one or the gym gyros one also train casual viewers: they know your videos have value *and* a funny moment, so they click again. The other side (Colin & Samir with Paddy): if a video looks like it's only joking around, it reads as low value. Show you've done the work, then be funny.

checks.q: Joke or observation: which works better?
checks.a: Humorous observations about what you're saying, ideally about yourself.

checks.q: The 5 types of humour from the book?
checks.a: Anecdotes/observations, analogies/metaphors, quotes, videos, photos.

reads.title: Made to Stick: why some ideas survive
reads.dek: Six principles, one popcorn story, and the curse that makes experts boring.
reads.md:
## The popcorn story
A health group wanted Americans to know movie popcorn was terrible. A medium bag had 37 g of saturated fat; the guideline was 20 g a day. A chart showing "nearly double" would have changed nothing.

Instead they said: a medium popcorn has more artery-clogging fat than a bacon-and-eggs breakfast, a Big Mac and fries for lunch, and a steak dinner with all the trimmings, **combined**. And they showed the food side by side. It was on every news channel, sales dropped, and cinemas switched oils. Fear, disgust and something from daily life made people care.

## Spotting good ideas
In a random basketball pick, you'd take the 7-foot guy. But a fast, trained 5'9" player beats a clumsy 7-footer. Learn to spot ideas with natural potential, then learn to make them great.

## The 6 principles (SUCCESs)
1. **Simple:** simple but profound. Be a master of exclusion: a video with 10 good ideas leaves no single one remembered.
2. **Unexpected:** counterintuitive. Surprise grabs attention short-term; open knowledge gaps and close them later to hold it.
3. **Concrete:** human actions and sensory detail.
4. **Credible:** why should they believe you?
5. **Emotional:** make them feel something. "37 g" does nothing; the popcorn picture does.
6. **Stories**

## The curse of knowledge
In one experiment, people tapped the rhythm of famous songs and listeners had to guess them. Tappers predicted 50% would be guessed. The real number: 3 out of 120. Once you know something, you can't imagine not knowing it.

So: **never underestimate the viewer's intelligence, and never overestimate his prior knowledge.** What sounds obvious to you can be brand new to him. Deep in a topic, you start valuing the specific stuff; he wants a simple answer to his problem.

## What is your core?
Southwest Airlines' core is "the cheap airline". Every decision asks one question: does this help us be the cheapest? Anyone can apply it in situations no one scripted. Compare "would Wizz Air want this?", which nobody can answer.

Your channel needs a core like that, one question every decision can be checked against.

## Compact ideas
Proverbs pack big ideas into a few words ("a bird in the hand…", "с един куршум два заека"). "Looksmaxxing" is one word for a whole topic. Say the core message early, and **tell the viewer which thing matters most**. One big thing gets remembered.

checks.q: The 6 principles?
checks.a: Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories.

checks.q: Southwest's core, and why it works?
checks.a: "The cheap airline": anyone can check any decision against it.

reads.title: 18 minutes and the Einstein test
reads.dek: Long enough to matter, short enough to keep attention, and simple enough to remember.
reads.md:
TED talks are capped at about 18 minutes. It's a rough rule, not a target for YouTube (in your niche data, 16–20 minutes did best on face channels, but length follows the content).

Thinking is tiring. A dense presentation drains people. (You may have read that willpower and thinking burn the same glucose. That "ego depletion" idea failed a large replication, so don't say it on camera. The point stands: lower the load.)

> "If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough."

Explaining a complex topic simply is something to aim for every time. People who don't do it are often scared of not showing everything they know. Your video isn't there to show the viewer how much you know. It's there to inform him in an easy and meaningful way.

And from the book's Part 3: **be courageous about your instincts and ideas**, or the things that could have been memorable get lost.

checks.q: Why do creators over-explain?
checks.a: They want to show everything they know, instead of informing the viewer simply.

reads.title: Intros: Paddy's 3 rules and the minute-3 test
reads.dek: How the first 30 seconds should work, from the strategist who has written about 10,000 intros.
reads.md:
## Paddy Galloway's 3 rules
1. **Confirm the click.** Whatever the thumbnail and title promised appears immediately.
2. **Contradiction / hook.**
3. **A seamless bridge** into the video (good to have, not required).

Bad bridge: "I'm going to show you 3 methods. Now let's get into it."
Good bridge: "I'm going to show you 3 methods, and the first one is to…"

## The minute-3 test
Stop someone at 3:00 and ask how they expect the video to continue. You want: "he's going to explain Y, at the end he shows X, and he mentioned Z so I want to see that too." Not: "I don't know, it just flows somewhere."

## Show it, don't just say it
Lots of people see your video on autoplay without sound before clicking. What they *see* in the first seconds decides it.

## An intro structure that works
Say you've been obsessed with the topic and studied it for a long time, and **show** it (more showing is better). Then reveal it's actually a simple N-step formula you'll walk through in the video.

## Educational vs entertainment
- Entertainment: the intro is the thumbnail, plus proof you're actually going to do it.
- Educational: tell the viewer why YOU are worth listening to. (Not always, but usually.)

After the click is confirmed, the rest of the intro opens a new curiosity gap, gives context and shows perceived effort. Perceived effort can be you saying how long you spent, or it can show in the editing and in how you talk. An open loop doesn't need to be a big mystery. "There are 3 steps" already creates one.

## Personality early
Show your personality in the first 15 seconds, so viewers know who they'll spend the next minutes with. Those who like it stay. But if it looks like you're only joking around, it reads as low value.

## Openers from speaking
- A question that matters to them: frame their problem as a question.
- A surprising fact that reframes the topic.

## Reframe so they care (Dan Mace)
How do you make people care about giving away shoes? MrBeast's line: "The only thing standing between these kids and an education is a simple pair of shoes… they walk for miles over harsh terrain, broken glass and contaminated water."

## Time
Spend about half your scripting time on the intro (Ali Abdaal; realistically about a third for you). But don't get lost in it. The viewer only sees it once, and studying what works beats polishing yours forever.

checks.q: Paddy's 3 intro rules?
checks.a: Confirm the click, contradiction/hook, seamless bridge.

checks.q: What should a viewer say at minute 3?
checks.a: "He'll explain Y, at the end he shows X, and he mentioned Z so I want that too."

reads.title: Every step is the most important one
reads.dek: Aprilynne's structure, the Hormozi lesson and the Oscar Patel rehook.
reads.md:
## Aprilynne's trick
Before the first point, say it's the most important one, because the biggest drop-off is at the start. The first point can be something that isn't strictly part of the topic. Yours: the most important step to debloating is being lean already. That isn't debloating, but if you're not lean, debloating won't show.

Aprilynne's video on killer intros:
- **Step 1, the most important:** packaging. Not part of the intro, but if they don't click, they never see the intro.
- **Step 2, "the most crucial part of the video":** the first 5 seconds. You're hooked again.
- **Step 3, "this is where it gets interesting":** the rest of the intro.
- **Step 4:** how to put it all together to go from okay to killer, so you can't skip it and still get what the title promised.

Every step is presented as the best one, in a different way.

## The Hormozi lesson
You watched a Hormozi presentation with parts 1, 2 and 3, part 3 being the most valuable. You didn't notice part 1 ending, and suddenly part 3 was starting. No dopamine from reaching the best part; you weren't invested. **When a video has steps, the viewer must always know where he is.**

## The Oscar Patel rehook
At 14:30 in Oscar Patel's 45-minute looksmaxxing video (20 Feb 2026), the science was getting boring. With higher energy he said something like: *"Let's go to habit 3. I know you're getting bored, I know you're getting lazy, but I need you to lock in. The better you look, the better you feel, the more opportunities you get… you owe it to yourself. I'm begging you, just take action."*

He re-hooked people by reminding them why they're watching: not for nothing, but to live a better life. And he begged them to **act**, not to keep watching, which feels genuine.

Use it in long guides. Your debloat plan already has it: "if you don't watch to the end your attention span is cooked" at the start, the lock-in moment mid-video, and every bit of value at the end.

checks.q: Why frame step 1 as the most important?
checks.a: The biggest drop-off is at the start, so that's where the hook goes.

checks.q: What did Oscar Patel ask viewers to do?
checks.a: Take action, not just keep watching. That's why it felt genuine.

reads.title: Bite-sized and simple
reads.dek: Two of your blue notes: split the video into small pieces, and respect what the viewer doesn't know yet.
reads.md:
## Bite-sized chunks
Spread the video in small pieces. Your carotenoid script wasn't split that way; your glow-up video was. A video with 4 points that split into sub-points, or 15 points, is easy to follow. One long point gets boring, especially if the words and sentences aren't simple.

## Never underestimate, never overestimate
**Never underestimate the viewer's intelligence. Never overestimate his prior knowledge.** He's smart and uninformed: don't talk down to him, don't over-explain obvious things, but do explain the *why*, because nobody has broken it down for him properly.

## Lower the cognitive load
When you watch YouTube, you want to rest a bit. Make learning feel like resting: a chill, satisfying explainer, not homework or an extreme teacher vibe. Let him sit back and enjoy it.

## Draw what he'd imagine
If you say something the viewer would picture in his head, show it on screen. His brain isn't at 100% while watching, so let it focus on what you're saying instead of imagining.

## Every line earns its place
- Don't repeat yourself. The audience wants new information.
- Ask: **does this move my story forward?**
- Don't waste the viewer's time. It's not about you, it's about them.
- Explain complex things simply. The job isn't to show what you know.

checks.q: The blue rule about the viewer's mind?
checks.a: Never underestimate his intelligence; never overestimate his prior knowledge.

checks.q: What's the one question for every line?
checks.a: Does this move my story forward?

reads.title: Underpromise, overdeliver
reads.dek: MrBeast's advice to Fabio Morena, and the A plot / B plot idea behind it.
reads.md:
This came from MrBeast's call with Fabio Morena. It's one of your purple notes. If you need it to hit hard, rewatch Fabio's video from 5 Sep 2026 up to 9:24.

## The idea
Title and thumbnail stay as strong as possible. But inside the video there's **so much more** than they promised.

The viewer who watched it loved it. He didn't expect that. He's used to clickbait, and you did the opposite. Now he's a fan, and years later he gets excited when someone mentions you. That's positive brand association, and it's how you get real fans. Use it whenever it fits.

Your veggie-tan idea is a good example: the packaging promises a better tan, and the video delivers the science, a real test and a lot more.

## A plot and B plot
- **The A plot** is the video's plot: what the packaging promises.
- **The B plot** is something extra the viewer didn't expect.

You can reveal the B plot in the intro or later in the video. You don't always need one, but it's "give them more": the opposite of clickbait. Viewers trust you more long term and leave more satisfied.

## Contrast makes it land
When you open a curiosity gap or a B plot, use contrast and emphasis (think Ryan Trahan). If the viewer doesn't notice the plot, the gap was never opened and there's nothing to close.

## The rest of the call
- **Do more, way more.** YouTube is in its best state ever. The opportunity is infinite.
- **Always be a student.** Out of everyone in the world, MrBeast called a creator far smaller than him for the chance of one small spark for a better video.
- **What are you bringing to the party?** If the party already has enough Finlandia vodka, they don't need yours. Bring the Jägermeister.

checks.q: What's the B plot?
checks.a: An extra the viewer didn't expect, beyond what the packaging promised.

checks.q: Why does over-delivering create fans?
checks.a: Viewers expect clickbait; getting more than promised makes them trust and remember you.

reads.title: One video, one feel
reads.dek: Packaging, intro, editing and script should all feel like they belong to the same video.
reads.md:
A blue note, and an easy one to forget mid-edit: **the packaging, intro, editing and script should all feel like they belong to the same video.** A playful thumbnail with a dry lecture, or a serious title with chaotic edits, breaks the promise.

## Stick to the core idea
Your note said to read this three times: stick to the core idea, for the channel and for the video.

## Think like a viewer as well as a creator
Use your creator brain to develop the idea, shape the story and make the video as good as possible. Then, before you commit, step outside all that context:
- What would I assume this video is about?
- What would make me choose it over everything else on the screen?
- Does the opening pay off what the packaging made me expect?

## Keep one style
Inside a video: one or at most two backgrounds, mostly the same text size, colour and font. If it's a static video, stay in one place. It feels much easier mentally.

checks.q: The blue rule about packaging, intro, editing and script?
checks.a: They should all feel like they belong to the same video.

reads.title: If they don't click, they don't watch
reads.dek: The fundamentals of titles and thumbnails, from pages 1 and 2 of your notes.
reads.md:
## Rule 1
YouTube isn't just a video platform. It's a **click-and-watch** platform. For someone to click, the video has to look valuable enough *and* create enough curiosity that he has no choice but to click.

- The way you word the packaging (and the intro) can matter as much as the video. It shapes the video.
- A good video doesn't equal views.
- The same video can look more or less valuable just from how it's packaged.

**Make the content niche, but the language broad.**

## The feed you're competing in
There's an abundance of choice. A viewer watches two kinds of creators: ones he's a fan of (you're new, so for now nobody's a fan yet) and new ones that stuck out with something too intriguing to skip. Picture how someone will discover your video (suggested next to which video?) and make yours the one he clicks.

## The curiosity gap
Imagine someone on his home page. How can your packaging scream "click me, I have information you NEED to know NOW"?

Make the viewer ask himself a big question he can't answer. Lots of low-view videos either answer the question in the packaging, or ask something everyone already knows.

- Is it intriguing enough for someone to spend the video's whole length on it?
- Could everyone watch it? Your mom, your little brother, an average guy, a mogger, a 37-year-old, a fan, a stranger?
- What's the most interesting way to word it?

## Don't cram
Beginners try to put the whole video in the title and thumbnail. Relax: create a gap and keep it minimal.

reads.title: Your title formats library
reads.dek: The formats from your notes, with why each one works.
reads.md:
## Bryan Ng's formats
- **"Y Is Designed to Fail"**: paranoia and victimhood. Viewers feel set up; you're the truth-teller. *Your Skincare Routine Is Designed to Fail.*
- **"The Most ___ in History, Explained"**: fascination with extremes plus a promise it's digestible.
- **"Z Is Hard, Until You…"**: validates the struggle, then promises a turning point. Viewers click to find the "until".
- **"I'm Politely Begging You To…"**: begging is desperate, polite is considerate; the contradiction makes people curious, and we want to help people who ask nicely.
- **"POV: You…"**: puts the viewer inside a scenario he'd never live. *POV: You Have to Glow Up in 2 Hours.*
- **"The Smartest Way to…"**: ego validation, and FOMO about choosing a dumber path.
- **"Watch Me Do X Live"**: expertise in action, nothing hidden.
- **"Give Me Z Minutes, I'll Show You How…"**

## Outliers you saved
- **"What [Authority] Won't Tell You (But I Will)"**: a 470× outlier. *What Looksmaxxers Won't Tell You (But I Will).*
- **"If You Don't Understand [hidden factor], You Don't Understand [goal]"**: "…Insulin… Fat Loss" got 250K+ views on a channel averaging ~1K.
- **"Y Is Better Than X"**: *Rice With Eggs Is Better Than Pizza* got 12M in 3 months.
- **"I Did Y Using Only This Method"**: a small Indian creator's 6-minute video hit 170K, 10× his next best.
- **"The Best Way to Stay Hydrated (Not Water)"**: 388K. Without the bracket it's maybe 10K.

## Word-level tricks
- Odd numbers feel real: $295 beats $300; "$45,000 a month" beats "$1 million".
- "Broke": *How MrBeast Broke YouTube*.
- "Complete opposites" beats "different".
- Lists beat how-to: 3 of 3 in Jake Thomas's tests (2.51% vs 1.90% CTR).
- "Change ___ Forever": *This Will Change the Way You Brush Your Teeth Forever*.
- "(They) Do THIS": *The Best Bodybuilders Do THIS*.
- Negativity: *Dumb Things Jeff Bezos Wastes His Billions On* (3.13%) beat *How Billionaire Jeff Bezos Spends All His Money* (2.30%).
- Extremes: add "-est".
- "Habit" beats "this"; "as a beginner" usually helps.

## More shapes to steal
*THE LAST [Topic] Guide You'll Ever Need* · *The N Types of…* · *The N Levels of Y in Z Minutes* · *The Secret to…* · *The #1 Cause of…* · *I Found It: The Perfect…* · *These N [Underrated] Do [Goal] Faster Than [Popular]* · *You're Not Behind (Yet)* · *This Stops [Problem] (and It Works Fast)* · *Every Free [Entity] You Actually Need, Explained in Y Minutes* · *Before You Start Training: 4 Smart Tips From a Gym Bro*

Copy the **structure**, never the exact phrase: your lab found that formulas burn out as more people use them.

checks.a: "What [Authority] Won't Tell You (But I Will)".

checks.q: Why does "Designed to Fail" work?
checks.a: Viewers feel set up (paranoia + victimhood) and you become the truth-teller.

reads.title: Thumbnail rules
reads.dek: Three elements, a one-second read, and the tests to run before you upload.
reads.md:
## Three core elements
To make a thumbnail quick to read, use **3 core elements** max. For example: a person, text with an arrow, and a dinosaur.

## Title and thumbnail talk to each other
- Good: title "The 3 Rules of YouTube", thumbnail "1. [a counterintuitive rule] 2. ████ 3. ████".
- Worst: title and thumbnail both say "The 3 Rules of YouTube". Wasted space, wasted reading.

## Paddy's extras
- Make it look like an **action**, like a frame you could press play on. Look like you're talking.
- For education, show a **process**.
- A few short, easy words. *You've been lied to.*
- The thumbnail doesn't have to appear in the video (a whiteboard in the thumbnail, no whiteboard in the video), as long as the promise is kept.
- Try a contradiction: *I found the cheapest GT3 RS… but no one wants to buy it.*

## Before you film
Sketch the thumbnail first, so you capture the shot.

## The glance test
Show it to someone for 2 seconds, then ask:
- What do you think this video is about?
- What stood out first?
- What do you remember?

If they can't answer, it isn't clear enough. Viewers don't study your thumbnail; they scroll past fast.

## Test macro, then micro
Make 3 **macro**-different thumbnails for an A/B/C test. Take the winner and make micro changes (shirt, object, word). Pick the best again.

## Steal from outside YouTube
Billboards are designed by people whose whole job is grabbing attention in one second. Look seriously at billboards, movie posters and TV shows. And keep an inspiration folder: screenshot packaging you like (thumbnails you could actually make), and write down *why* you like it.

## Ideas you saved
- "This made me…" with an arrow to something you can't quite see. Huge curiosity.
- "You've won" next to a "How to Win at…" title.
- Every 4th video or so, try packaging that's completely your own.

checks.q: The glance-test questions?
checks.a: What's it about? What stood out first? What do you remember?

checks.q: How do you A/B test thumbnails?
checks.a: 3 macro-different concepts first, then micro changes on the winner.

reads.title: Editing for emotion, not effects
reads.dek: Fewer cuts, music that follows the story, and a deadline you set yourself.
reads.md:
## Stop impressing, start clarifying
- A faster video isn't a better video. Stop making so many cuts.
- Don't put anything in that you wouldn't want to see in someone else's video.
- Don't try to impress with editing skills. Make it watchable.
- If an edit looks good but the information is too fast or cluttered to follow, delete it.
- Skip trendy, overused elements you wouldn't like elsewhere (the 5-coloured-levels thumbnails, the green-vs-red split screens). Gut feeling.
- Simple but modern.

## Edit for emotion
What should the viewer feel here? You want edits that cause involuntary emotional reactions and that people can't stop thinking about. Not fancy effects: the psychology of what makes people feel something.

## Music and sound
- When the video moves to a new point, the music (and the timestamp) should show it. The music follows the story.
- Use sound effects sparingly: movement gets a sound, emphasis gets a sound. **Silence** for a moment makes the emphasis land.
- **Leitmotif:** a recurring sound or music cue tied to one idea, feeling, place or character (Ryan Trahan's "da mountain"). Even 2 seconds works.
- For a big point: cut the music with a crash zoom on your face, then bring it back 2 seconds later.
- A tension riser into the intro's end, then a hit.
- When switching songs, use the timed version from Epidemic so the first one ends on time.

## Reuse and repeat
Build animations you can reuse, like one timeline in Fusion that you zoom into. It reminds viewers what happened before and saves time.

## Contrast
Contrast creates focus: within 2 seconds, within a section, between two things in the whole video (Ryan Trahan's modern Meta glasses in an old van), and between your video and the rest of the niche.

## Ship it (blue)
To make a video faster, set a **self-imposed deadline**: "the deadline is Monday". Realistic, but a bit hard.

## The intro gets extra care
Really focus on the intro, both the editing and the making of it. Re-record it if you can.

reads.title: Obsess over ideas, not analytics
reads.dek: A purple note from many top creators, plus your "REALLY IMPORTANT" one about idea time.
reads.md:
## The purple rule
Many successful creators say the same thing: **instead of obsessing over analytics, obsess over good ideas.** Your strategist research agrees. The order is idea, then packaging, then the first 30 seconds, then everything else. "A good video cannot rescue a bad idea."

## Your "REALLY IMPORTANT" note
Take a lot more time on the idea and *how* you'll make the video. The tier list in your first video changed it completely. Write several versions with different angles and pick the best.

## Paddy's hallmarks of a great idea
- Interesting to the **core, casual and new** audience
- **Easy to convey** in a title and thumbnail
- **Unique / novelty** value
- **Combines** one or more viral formats
- **Friends get excited** when you mention it

## Be where your competition isn't
Combine genres. Yours: how to be attractive, but **cinematic and with jokes**, two things barely present in this niche. You're not the best attractiveness channel or the most cinematic channel, but you can be the best cinematic attractiveness channel for young guys. The other version: use advantages you have, like being young and having an aesthetic body.

## What does the niche lack visually?
Do they sit in dark rooms? Light rooms? Is the editing trash, or extreme? Do they sit still or film outside too much? Do the opposite if it makes sense. Take elements from creators you love, the parts that make them feel different, and over time you become unique.

## Interested is interesting (Dan Mace)
Everyone has seen a double rainbow. That video went viral because of the man's reaction. Casey Neistat's videos about anything get millions of views because he's so interested. Stress less about "will people find this interesting?" and more about "how interested am I?"

## Talk to your viewers
Ask guys in your target audience: what do they want to learn about attractiveness, why do they want it, do they think it's possible, why don't they watch videos about it, and what would they want those videos to look like?

checks.a: Obsess over good ideas instead of analytics.

reads.dek: Your purple note from Zornica at Teenovator, plus the promise every fan relies on.
reads.md:
## Be the example (purple)
From Zornica at Teenovator: **personal brand = what you do + what you believe in + how they remember you.**
- To sell something, you have to be the example. If you sell attractiveness coaching, you must always look attractive, anywhere people find you. That's integrity: what you do and what you say are the same.
- Have a story people resonate with: why you wanted to become attractive. There's a deeper meaning behind it. Let the audience know it.
- Start building a name before you're famous. Instagram can show you eating healthy, training, trying things, so people trust you before you ever sell anything.
- Authenticity matters a lot. Be yourself, even if you look a bit stupid.
- The right question isn't "what do I want to say?" but **"why would someone want to hear it?"**
- A motto you wrote: *we become more attractive so we can live a better life.*

## Every video
Every video should bring him one step closer to what he wants (becoming more attractive), and he should trust you as much as possible. Ask: **does this make them trust me more or less?**

He doesn't really care about you. He cares about becoming more attractive, and you're entertaining and helping him. Even core fans who feel connected mostly care about what they get. (You don't care how Pierre Dalati's day went; you care what he does on an average day because you could learn from it.) Keep it enjoyable for you and useful for him.

## Your channel promise
**"I will help you become more attractive."** Fans and viewers are different. Fans click no matter the packaging because they trust the promise. To earn that, keep the promise in every video.

## Reputation
What do people think when they hear your name? What emotion do you drive? Is it premium? Everything has to fit the identity: what you wear, your sponsors, your music, your room. Ask: **is this on brand?**

## Your mission
To a future team, don't say "I want a million subs". Say: we're on a mission to teach the world about attractiveness, help millions of young men become their best selves and get what they want in life, and transform the attractiveness-channel industry.

reads.title: Building a cult-like audience
reads.dek: How to become someone's favourite creator in the niche, and why the Discord matters.
reads.md:
## The 7 ingredients
1. **A common enemy.** Yours: blackpill and extreme looksmaxxing. Three contrasts: mental health (they get depressed about their looks, you do the opposite), physical health (only safe methods), legitimacy (only methods proven to work).
2. **A very specific niche.** The more specific, the more a viewer admires a creator in it. Yours: healthy attractiveness from a male teen, for male teens.
3. **Give the viewer ownership:** polls on the next video, answering comments, the Discord.
4. **He wants to be you:** a better version of himself he'd like to become.
5. **You're his bro:** he feels like you're similar and like a friend (how you felt about Hamza at 13).
6. **Being funny as hell**
7. **Recurring jokes and things**

## Who you're talking to
He's around 17–18, average-looking, motivated but lost. Girls are on his mind. Status is on his mind. He isn't sad where he is; he just knows he could be better and wants someone to show him how. Self-improvement content has felt too vague, or made for someone older and richer.
- Direct, no fluff. Say **"you"**, not "guys".
- Smart but uninformed: explain the why.
- Slightly ahead of him, not miles ahead.
- Say what he actually wants out loud sometimes: girls noticing him, guys respecting him.

## Stranger clicks, loyal viewer stays
**Package every video for a stranger to click, but film every video for the 16-year-old who's been watching since the start.** Over time the stranger becomes the loyal viewer, but only if there's something to belong to. Make each video standalone, but talk like it's part of something bigger.

## Make it interactive
Interactive media is the future. For others that's streaming; for you it's the Discord.
- Make videos that answer the community: "you guys asked me in the Discord about X, so here's the full breakdown."
- "We've been talking about this in the Discord" makes it feel alive and makes new viewers want in.
- Use community posts and polls early: "What's harder for you, diet or gym consistency?"

## Airrack's warning
You need a community to hit a million. He says he could easily make a 50M-view video that doesn't build community. Consistently serve the right audience. The rubber-band video might work, but is it your community? Empty views that never buy don't help much beyond AdSense. The future is smaller creators with their own niche and audience.

Always ask: **would 80% of this video's viewers also watch my other videos?**

checks.a: Blackpill/extreme looksmaxxing: mental health, physical health, legitimacy.

checks.q: Package for whom, film for whom?
checks.a: Package for a stranger, film for the 16-year-old who's watched since the start.

reads.title: Make it a show
reads.dek: People binge shows. Turn videos into series that feel like one thing.
reads.md:
All the big creators make shows. *50 States in 50 Days* is a show, and people binge-watch shows.
- The videos look and feel alike. The thumbnail doesn't have to say it's a show, but give a cue: a repeating song, or saying it's part of a series.
- A show like Ryan Trahan's runs back to back, with no other videos in between.

## Show ideas from your notes
- **Every glow-up method, one per video:** hair, lips, breath, smell, fragrance, style, eyebrows, skincare, BB cream…
- **I test an attractiveness method for N days** (jawliner gum, neck curls, retinoid, azelaic acid). These can't be back to back, so they go in a playlist. Playlists get watched less, so give it the power of a show: **at the end of every test, rate it 1–10**, so the series becomes one tier list split across videos and viewers want to see them all.
- **Category runs:** an explainer first, then a block of videos with one thumbnail colour scheme (green for leanness, food and bloating; orange for colouring like brows and carotenoids), then the next category. It could be its own channel or a playlist series.
- Name series like *Increasing attractiveness through…*, e.g. one fragrance per video.

## Repeat objects (Dan Mace)
Casey Neistat's glasses with white paint, Nas Daily's same shirt. Once something becomes tied to a feeling viewers liked, it carries that feeling into every video. What object, outfit or set piece could you repeat?

## A long hub video
Make one very long video, like a full 50-minute guide, and point lots of other videos to it. A 5-minute video doesn't make a fan; 50 minutes with you does. That's how Bryan Ng made you a fan, down to his newsletter. Mention the Discord inside it in small pieces.

checks.a: Rate each method 1–10 at the end, so the series becomes one tier list.

reads.title: The 3 metrics and how to upload
reads.dek: CTR, view duration and returning viewers, plus the upload routine and how creators really earn.
reads.md:
## The 3 most important metrics
1. **CTR (click-through rate).** On upload, aim for over 5%. Under 5% early: ask whether the video is actually good. A year later, under 5% is fine, because it's being shown to lots of new people.
2. **AVD (average view duration).** On a 12-minute video you want over 50%.
3. **Returning viewers.** The community metric. If it's low, ask: am I targeting a different identity every video? Build for one specific person who'd watch most of your videos. How do you make him come back?

Right after publishing, with a core audience watching first: 5–10% CTR and ~70% still watching at 30 seconds is very good. And when people click, their expectations are high. Never disappoint them; they're giving you their time.

Your strategist research adds: don't panic in the first 48 hours, watch positive comments per view, and judge a format over 10–15 videos, not one.

## Upload routine
- Upload as **unlisted** first so YouTube can process and understand it. Create a community post and publish it as the video goes public, so fans get notified better. (Community post notifications are limited to about one every 3 days.)
- After uploading, don't watch your own video unless you watch to the end. It hurts the average view duration.

## How creators actually earn (Aprilynne)
She links her gear under every video as Amazon affiliate links, but that earns little. Programs like Epidemic Sound pay her 50% of revenue every month. She earns most from sponsorships that come with an affiliate link.

## Reputation is a metric too
What do people think when they hear your name, in a YouTube context? Every decision (clothes, music, sponsors, room) either fits the brand or doesn't.

checks.q: The 3 most important metrics?
checks.a: CTR, average view duration, returning viewers.

checks.q: Why upload unlisted first?
checks.a: So YouTube processes and understands it before it goes public.

reads.title: Building and motivating a team
reads.dek: How MrBeast trains people, who to hire, and how to talk about the mission.
reads.md:
## Train like MrBeast
Spend a huge amount of time with the person who'll work for you. Show them every little detail. They watch what you do for months, even years, until they become like you. Then that person trains 3 more people the same way. It's a big investment, but advice and books don't teach anyone this. (That's the extreme version; MrBeast did it.)

## Who to hire
1. **Coachability:** able and eager to learn everything. YouTube is ultra-specific; whoever it is will have a lot to learn.
2. **Real interest in the channel's topic.**
3. **Wanting to do more:** passionate, hard-working, and wanting to go further with you. The editor today could be a manager later.

Talk Like TED adds: hire for passion.

## How to talk about it
Not "I want a million subs". Say: *we're on a mission to educate the world on attractiveness, help millions of young men become their best selves and get what they want in life. We're going to transform the attractiveness-channel industry, and we'll do it by showing up and changing how young men see themselves.*

And pitch with a story (your BUas editor pitch): learn on a real channel, from someone who has done it, with real viewer feedback, for free, and real money if you stick with it.

## Working together (Ali Abdaal)
- Working in a team is proven to be a lot better. Hold each other accountable, don't race each other. Make it so that you working means everyone wins.
- Stay in sync. If both of you work hard, you like each other. If one coasts, you get angrier than if you'd been alone (you learned this at Teenovator).
- Even working on different things next to each other helps focus.
- Some people drain energy, some give it. Find the givers.

checks.q: Top 3 hiring traits?
checks.a: Coachability, real interest in the topic, wanting to go further.

reads.title: The reward is getting to make it
reads.dek: Your most-marked note: three purple circles and "EXTREMELY IMPORTANT".
reads.md:
## Your note, almost word for word
When I make a video, I like making the video. **My reward is that I GET to make it**, every part of it. Views and comments are a separate bonus, not the real reward.

The reward is the effort I put in. That effort made me grow, and growth is the most valuable thing.

Views don't decide whether I'm doing well. I know whether I'm doing well: I know how much effort I've put in, and where. I have more than the views. I have the skills and the growth to get the higher views later.

The number doesn't matter. What matters is that I know I'm growing. Growth means two things: **I'm putting in effort, and I'm putting it in the right place.**

## Why it's backed by research
- **The reward trap (blue in your notes).** People told they'd be paid for solving puzzles spent less of their free time on them afterwards than people who were never paid (Deci 1971; your notes call it the Rubik's cube study). Kids who loved drawing and then got rewards for it drew less once the rewards stopped (Lepper 1973). Make it a game, not a paycheck.
- **Huberman's version:** don't think about the reward while doing hard work. Learn to enjoy the effort itself. Don't run 5 km "for a cake"; you'll quit. (The "it raises your baseline dopamine" part is his idea, not proven.)
- **Ali Abdaal:** do it for the process. Ideating, packaging, scripting, filming, editing, analysing: that's what you love. Money and connections are a bonus that comes later. Focus on the result and you won't enjoy the process, because the result comes much later.

## Not all outcome goals are equal
Jack builds a business to reach $1M so he's financially free and can provide for his family. Mike builds one to reach $1M so his dad isn't disappointed. Both chase an outcome, but Jack is more likely to get there and happier when he does.

## When the work is boring
Ask: **"What would this look like if it were fun?"** Add music, humour, a creative element, friends, a treat at the end.

checks.a: Putting in effort, and putting it in the right place.

checks.a: Once the rewards stopped, they drew less than before.

reads.title: Why not more?
reads.dek: MrBeast's question, your note from the night you built the game, and how to answer it without breaking yourself.
reads.md:
## The question
Imagine MrBeast asks you right now: **"But why don't you work more?"** Answer it honestly.

YouTube is in its best state ever and the opportunity is infinite. You can become absolutely great. Every chance you have, do more. And always be a student: MrBeast called someone far smaller than him for the chance of one spark.

## Your own proof
The night you built the strategy game, you worked from 8 pm until 12:20 am because it was interesting. That proves you can work long hours when you're into something. So drop the limiting thoughts:
- "Oh, but 90 minutes have passed."
- "I shouldn't start a session, I only have 40 minutes."

No. Do as much as possible. Play the game of YouTube. That's the real game.

## Work in the now
Don't think "did I get views this month?" or "was that choice good?". 99% of the time, think: **am I doing something right now?** Do the task of the now. When it's all done, look back and fix what needs fixing. Today you have to use your real free time well. What matters is whether you work today.

## The honest edge
More hours, same bedtime. The interest is what kept you going until 12:20; the lesson is to make the work interesting, not to cut sleep. Your own research says sleep loss makes people look less attractive and learn worse, and your channel teaches exactly that. Breaks help too: taking one when you're fading makes you work more and better.

checks.q: MrBeast's question to answer every day?
checks.a: "Why don't you work more?"

checks.q: What should you think about 99% of the time?
checks.a: Am I doing something right now?

reads.title: You become what you repeat
reads.dek: Neuroplasticity, errors, and why a weak video is a heavy set.
reads.md:
My brain becomes what I repeat.

That's neuroplasticity. Every time I do something, the path for it in my brain gets a little stronger, and every time I skip it, a different path gets stronger instead. I'm always training something. The only question is what.

I already know this works, because I built my body the same way. Not in one workout, but through years of showing up, adding weight and failing reps. Skills grow the same way.

So when the work feels hard, that's the heavy set. That's the rewiring happening. Mistakes aren't proof I'm bad at this; they're how my brain learns. Every weak video I make builds the good one.

Andrew Huberman: **"Errors are the basis for neuroplasticity and learning."** If you want to rewire your brain, make more errors (with feedback, so you learn from them).

Every hour I put in today makes me better. Neuroplasticity rewards repetition, not intention.

checks.q: What does neuroplasticity reward?
checks.a: Repetition, not intention.

reads.title: Ali Abdaal's toolkit
reads.dek: The practical tools from Feel-Good Productivity, in one place.
reads.md:
## Before you start something
- **The 5 whys.** Ask "why?" five times. By the fifth, the answer should connect to something important long term. If it doesn't (watching a Minecraft video → "it gives me dopamine"), skip it.
- **Then ask how.** Not knowing exactly what to do drains energy and wastes time.
- **NICE goals:** Near-term, Input-based, Controllable, Energizing. Don't think too much about the long-term goal while working, or you won't enjoy the short-term work.
- **The pre-mortem:** a week has passed and you haven't started. What are the 3 main reasons? How can you reduce each? Who can help you stay on it? What can you do right now?
- **If you don't know when you'll do it, you probably won't.** Time-block it: "scripting the skincare video", not "YouTube time".

## When you're stuck
- **What's the next step?** The smallest physical action. Exam: open the book. Gym: put your shoes on. Script: open Notion.
- **The 5-minute rule.** Do it for 5 minutes. After 5 you're actually allowed to stop (otherwise you'll know the rule is a lie). Usually you'll keep going.
- **Short-term goals.** "Edit the intro today" feels much easier than "upload the video this week", even though it's the same plan.
- **"I don't have to do this perfectly. I should just start."** MrBeast has to be perfect now; in his first 10 years he just had to start.
- **Fear:** ask "what am I feeling, and why am I scared?" It's how the 6-metre jump goes from 10 minutes to 10 seconds. Ali wanted to post in 2010 and posted in 2017.
- **Unblock, don't force.** Take the stone out of your shoe instead of running to dinner bleeding.

## Your mind
- **Labels.** You act like the label you give yourself. You're not a procrastinator. You worked a job to buy a camera, listened to YouTube podcasts at work, moved rooms to film. Hard-working person. Get to work.
- **Forgive yourself.** Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating procrastinated less next time (Wohl 2010). "I didn't do X, but I did Y."
- **10/10/10.** Will it matter in 10 minutes, 10 weeks, 10 years?
- **The projector effect.** You think everyone's watching and judging you. They're busy with themselves.
- **Ownership.** Not "I have to", but "I choose to": I choose to work on YouTube because I want it.
- **Alter ego.** Use one when you need it (yours are in your "alter e" note).
- **Track progress.** Write it down. You'll see where you're weak and that you're improving.
- **Accountability buddy** (r/GetMotivatedBuddies), with clear agreements.
- **Teach to learn.** Teaching others is proven to beat learning alone.

checks.q: What are NICE goals?
checks.a: Near-term, Input-based, Controllable, Energizing.

checks.q: The 4 pre-mortem questions?
checks.a: 3 reasons you didn't start; how to reduce each; who can help; what to do now.

reads.dek: Conserve, say no, take real breaks, and don't use willpower on things that don't matter.
reads.md:
## Say no
One cause of burnout is hyper-engagement. Steve Jobs said no to a lot. When he came back as CEO, he killed a project Apple had worked on for 5 years. **"Saying no is just as important as saying yes."**
- Say no more often to things that don't help the channel. Want to get good at chess? No, focus on the channel.
- Example: no Teenovator or Able Mentor this year.
- If you wouldn't do it tomorrow, don't say yes to it six weeks from now. You'll be busy then too.

## Distractions, controlled
If you lost time to distractions, don't abandon your goals. Snap back. Zero distractions leads to burnout; many or big distractions mean no progress. Tired of the work? Go outside for 10 minutes, do push-ups, listen to one song, then go back.

A widely shared figure from app tracking data says the most productive people worked about 52 minutes and rested about 17. It's observational, not a controlled study, but the lesson holds: when you're losing focus after a long stretch, a break doesn't just feel better. It makes you work more and better. Don't "I'm disciplined" your way through when you need a break.

## Don't do too many things
Trying to do YouTube while also keeping a Duolingo streak, going to Teenovator every Thursday, juggling a ball 30 minutes a day, learning to cook and getting good grades is a recipe for burnout. If something isn't related to YouTube or the niche, don't force yourself to get good at it (school grades aside). Try interesting things for fun, but don't spend discipline on them.

checks.a: If you wouldn't do it tomorrow, you'll be just as busy then.

- **Help others.** Volunteers like volunteering; MrBeast likes helping. Helping makes you feel good (and gives you a reason to work harder), which is one reason you like your niche.

- **Find people who give you energy**, and avoid the ones who drain it.
- **Get friends doing similar things:** YouTuber or media friends at your level or ahead, people who eat clean and care about looking good.
- **Socialise without wasting time.** Play Dune (MrBeast's favourite board game) or Diplomacy (Elon Musk's). They train skills that transfer to YouTube.

reads.title: Huberman: what you should actually do
reads.dek: The parts of your Huberman notes worth acting on, with honest evidence notes.
reads.md:
## 1. Resist urges
When you look at tasty junk food and don't buy it, you train the same skill that stops you from arguing or opening Instagram. You wrote: if you only take one thing from the podcast, make it this.

## 2. How to do hard work
Don't think about the reward while working. The hard work is the reward. Friction you push through is how you grow. Don't spike dopamine right before or after effort; learn to enjoy the effort itself. (Whether this raises your "baseline dopamine" isn't proven, but the reward research supports the idea of enjoying the process.)

## 3. Focus
Close your eyes and focus on your breathing and the feeling of your skin. The study behind this (Basso 2019) used **13 minutes a day for 8 weeks** to improve attention. One session doesn't do the long-term part.

## 4. Morning light
Go outside within the first hour of waking, or open the window and stick your head out, for 5–20 minutes. It helps alertness and sleep timing. (The testosterone claim is weak; don't put it on camera.)

## 5. Water on waking
500 ml–1 L of water when you wake up. Good for debloating and getting going.

## 6. Late screens
Limit bright screens in the hour before bed. Blue-light glasses barely help (Cochrane review 2023), so lower brightness and screen time instead. Your work matters more than perfect sleep hygiene, so dim things when you can.

## Not actions, just info
- Anything hard you do without quitting teaches your brain to do hard things. The opposite is also true.
- The "eye-movement trick to fall asleep fast" has no evidence behind it that I could find.
