reads.title: Bloat vs fat: the science of a puffy face
reads.dek: What's actually happening when your face looks fatter in the morning, and what helps.
reads.md:
## Water, not fat
Fat takes weeks or months to change. Water changes in a day. If your face looks slimmer at night than in the morning, that's water. That's why debloating is so useful: it's one of the few looks changes you can see the next day.

## Salt
Sodium is the main lever. More salt than usual makes your body hold more water for a while, and for many guys the face shows it first. It's water, so it comes off in days.
- Average intake worldwide is about **4,300 mg** of sodium a day.
- The WHO limit is **under 2,000 mg** (5 g of salt).
- Half a takeaway pizza can already pass the whole day's limit. Restaurants are often saltier than fast food, and packaged food carries most of it.

## Potassium
Potassium makes your kidneys excrete more sodium, so it helps your body get rid of the salt. Bananas, potatoes, beans, avocado.

## Carbs
Each gram of glycogen (stored carbs) holds about 3 g of water, and insulin tells the kidneys to hold on to sodium. Where salt stays, water stays. Carbs aren't bad; a big carb-and-salt dinner just shows up on your face in the morning.

## Alcohol and sleep
Alcohol blocks the hormone that holds water (vasopressin), so you pee more, then rebound. Lying flat lets fluid settle in your face overnight; standing and moving drains it during the day.

## Movement
Seated calf raises after a meal cut the blood-sugar spike by about half (Hamilton 2022). That's about blood sugar. It isn't proven to debloat your face directly.

## Quick fixes
Ice, cold water and gua sha depuff for a few hours. They're short-term fixes before a photo, not long-term change.

## What doesn't work
You can't spot-reduce face fat. A face slims through overall fat loss plus less water retention.

checks.q: How do you tell bloat from fat?
checks.a: Water changes in a day (puffier mornings, slimmer nights); fat takes weeks.

checks.q: What does potassium do?
checks.a: Helps the kidneys get rid of sodium.

reads.title: Myth check: gum, mewing, hunter eyes, face yoga
reads.dek: The honest answers to what your viewers keep asking.
reads.md:
## Jawline gum
It raises bite force. The best young-adult trial (Jung 2024, 58 people, 6 months) found **no change in masseter size or jaw shape**. The "pump" after chewing is a contracted muscle (around 56% thicker than relaxed), so it disappears. Heavy use can cause jaw (TMJ) pain and headaches. Jaw definition mostly comes down to body fat.

## Mewing
No controlled evidence that it reshapes bone in adults. Normal tongue posture is harmless. Hard mewing and bone smashing carry risk for no proven benefit.

## Hunter eyes
Eye shape is mostly bone, fat and genetics. No exercise or mewing has evidence for changing it. What you *can* change: puffiness and dark circles (sleep, salt) and groomed brows.

## Face yoga and face exercises
No spot reduction. The one small study (Alam 2018, middle-aged women) showed **fuller** upper cheeks, which isn't a slimmer face.

## Raising your hyoid bone
No non-surgical evidence.

## Power poses, ego depletion, blue-light glasses
- Power posing doesn't change hormones (Ranehill 2015).
- "Willpower runs on glucose" failed a 23-lab replication.
- Blue-light glasses barely help sleep.

## Why this matters for you
Every one of these is a chance to be the honest voice in a niche full of hype. It's also your common enemy at work: extreme, unproven, sometimes harmful methods.

checks.q: What did the best gum RCT find?
checks.a: No change in masseter size or jaw shape after 6 months.

checks.q: What can you actually change around the eyes?
checks.a: Puffiness, dark circles and brow grooming. Not the shape.

reads.title: Skin: acne, retinoids and the veggie tan
reads.dek: What works for acne, how long it takes, and why carrots can change your skin colour.
reads.md:
## Acne
- Face washes are rarely the fix.
- A topical **retinoid** (adapalene is available without prescription in many places) is first-line. Benzoyl peroxide helps too.
- Give it **8–12 weeks**. The first couple of weeks can look worse. That's normal, and it's where most people quit.
- Expect irritation: moisturise, and wear sunscreen every day.
- See a dermatologist if it's severe or scarring.

## Post-acne marks
Azelaic acid is decent for brown marks (PIH) and acne itself. Evidence is weaker for pink/red marks (PIE), so don't promise "ASAP".

## The veggie tan
Carotenoids from fruit and vegetables build up in your skin. Within about **6 weeks** of eating more of them, skin looks more golden, and people rate it healthier and more attractive (Whitehead 2012). In those studies, carotenoid colour was preferred over melanin (tan) colour (Stephen 2011). Eat a variety of colourful fruit and veg, not just carrots. Only extreme amounts turn you orange.

## Sleep shows on your face
Sleep-deprived people were rated less attractive and more tired-looking (Axelsson 2010; Sundelin 2017). Sleep is the cheapest looks upgrade there is.

## Facial contrast
Most facial-contrast research is on women's faces. In men it's linked more to looking younger and healthier. Say what's known and what isn't.

checks.q: How long until a retinoid works?
checks.a: About 8–12 weeks, and it can look worse first.

checks.q: How long until the veggie tan shows?
checks.a: About 6 weeks.

reads.title: Why you look worse in photos
reads.dek: Two real reasons, and how to fix both.
reads.md:
## 1. Lens distortion
At selfie distance (about 30 cm), the camera makes your nose look roughly **30% wider** than at 1.5 m (Ward 2018). Your face looks rounder and more distorted than it really is.

**Fix:** hold the phone further away and zoom in (2×), or use the back camera on a timer.

## 2. You're used to your mirror face
You see your flipped face every day in the mirror, so it feels "right". The camera shows the real version, which feels slightly off to *you* but looks normal to everyone else. That's the mere-exposure effect (Mita 1977).

## Also
- **Light:** face a window. Overhead light makes shadows under your eyes.
- **Angle:** camera slightly above eye level.
- **Bloat:** morning photos after a salty dinner show it. Shoot later in the day.

Photo and "photogenic" questions are about 5% of all teen looks posts and rising, so this is a video waiting to be made.

checks.q: How much wider does the nose look at selfie distance?
checks.a: About 30% wider than at 1.5 m.

checks.q: Why do you prefer your mirror face?
checks.a: Mere exposure: you see the flipped version every day.

reads.title: The strategists' 60-second version
reads.dek: What the best YouTube strategists believe right now: your 102-video report, condensed.
reads.md:
1. **The idea is the video.** Nearly every serious strategist, including Paddy, Jake Trinder, Vexian, Grant Rodahl, Jake Bryant and Kallaway, ranks it in this order: idea/topic, then packaging, then the first 30 seconds, then everything else. "A good video cannot rescue a bad idea."
2. **Validate demand before you film.** Outliers are your evidence, and an outlier from a *small* channel is worth more than one from a big channel. A single outlier doesn't prove anything; a pattern that shows up across several channels does.
3. **Borrow the topic from inside your niche and the packaging from outside it.** This is the most-repeated advanced idea of the season (Trinder, Paddy, Brent from 1of10, Jake Bryant, Kallaway, Dan the creator).
4. **YouTube is click-and-watch, not served.** Your title and thumbnail are the whole entry ticket. Thumbnails are getting bigger and titles smaller on every surface, so the thumbnail has to create interest by itself.
5. **The first 30 seconds is a contract.** Confirm the click, give a promise, proof and a plan, make it personal, open a new loop and set expectations. Then deliver value fast.
6. **Satisfaction beats retention.** YouTube says its north star is "long-term user value", measured partly with surveys. Jake Trinder's best video had about 12% retention and 932K views. Your best leading indicator is positive comments per view.
7. **Commit to one format for 10–15 videos before judging it.** "A channel of single attempts is no data."
8. **The platform changed this autumn.** Views now count from the first frame, so "engaged views" are the real number. YPP for new channels doubles in Feb 2027 to 8,000 watch hours. Shows/seasons, dynamic thumbnails, video A/B tests, the research tab that now surfaces outliers, and Ask YouTube are all arriving. There's a crackdown on reuploads, AI "experts" and clickbait.
9. **Authentic and human is the counter-AI moat.** People want a recognisable person, a format and a belief system they can belong to.

reads.title: Where strategists agree, and where they argue
reads.dek: 12 shared principles and 9 live debates, with a verdict for your channel on each.
reads.md:
## Where the best agree
1. **Ideas > packaging > intro > everything else.** Production upgrades come last. Paddy's pendulum, Jake Bryant's "5/10 content then 10/10 packaging" and Shaan's "A+ content with C- delivery" all say the same thing.
2. **Demand evidence before effort.** Look for outliers at 3–5x or more, prefer *small* channels and *recent* videos, look for repeated patterns over single hits, and check that views are organic (comments in proportion to views).
3. **Cross-niche packaging.** Keep the topic in your niche and take the format, composition and title psychology from adjacent niches with the same viewers or intent. "Similar enough to belong, different enough to catch the eye" (Brent).
4. **A thumbnail is a question or an emotion, readable in one second**, and the title complements it without repeating it. Do the squint test, the 50% TV test, the cover-the-text test and the two-second glance.
5. **Confirm the click immediately.** Whatever is in the thumbnail should be on screen in the first seconds (Royalty Family went from 12M to 25M when they started doing this).
6. **Make it personal.** Have a guide on camera and a reason why *you* care. This matters more and more as a defence against AI.
7. **Stakes and structure.** A character who wants something, an obstacle, rising stakes, re-hooks and but/therefore beats. Even tutorials can be wrapped as stories.
8. **Commit to a format** for 10–15 videos and double down on winners three times in a row. Don't change a hit's format just because you're bored of it.
9. **Watch views, curve shapes and positive comments per view.** Don't obsess over CTR. Never panic in the first 48 hours.
10. **Be a student of YouTube:** keep reference playlists and boards, study daily, and run post-mortems after every video, both hits and flops.
11. **Packaging and audience change over a video's life.** Rescue old videos with new thumbnails (Aprilynne's examples went from 35 to 800 views an hour), and use dynamic thumbnails as they roll out.
12. **Build a belief system and community**, not just an audience: a name, rituals, an enemy, sacred words.

## Live debates, and the verdict for you
| Debate | Side A | Side B | Verdict for you |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A/B testing on small channels** | Jake Bryant: test from day one; he has receipts. Paddy: build the 3-thumbnail *muscle*. | Trinder: it splits data at low views and slows learning. MKBHD and the vidIQ hosts: it kills confidence. | **Make 3 genuinely different thumbnails, publish your best, and only run a test when you're truly torn.** Never test colour variants. |
| **Retention vs satisfaction** | Editing gurus: retention is everything. | Trinder: 12% retention gave 932K. YouTube uses surveys. moneymaxxing: "retention is bullsh*t". | **Satisfaction.** Shorten the time to value. Edit to clarify, not to decorate. |
| **Upload frequency** | Nate Curtis, Jade, Molly: volume and consistency. Aprilynne: a quantity arc while you're searching. | Grant, Royalty Family, Jake Bryant, Trinder: fewer, better videos; every other week can beat weekly. | At your stage, 2 a month is **too slow to learn from**. Do a 3-month burst of weekly uploads in one format, then return to 2 a month at higher quality. |
| **Niche vs broad** | Paddy: start narrow and expand. Brent and Kallaway: narrow buyers. | Nate Curtis: "niche is propaganda", brand is the moat. Nate Black: over-narrowing caps you. | Keep a **narrow promise** (science-based attractiveness for average young men) and **broad topics inside it**. That's Paddy's Core/Casual/New and Aprilynne's 80% rule. |
| **Outliers: copy or not** | vidIQ, MonomoTime, 1of10: the outlier method works. | Dan the creator claims YouTube scores similarity. Chucky (MrBeast): repeat content won't perform. | Copy the **psychology and format**, never the words. Add your originality at the outlier's selling point. Prefer outliers from adjacent niches. |
| **SEO** | Adam Ivy: search never expires; Ask YouTube makes intent matter more. | Paddy: search is 5–10% of traffic and SEO titles are garbage. | Write for **browse** and suggested. For a few evergreen "how to fix X" videos, use natural question language. |
| **Dubbing** | Aprilynne: 5x engaged views with her own voice. Dan: go global-first. | Adam Ivy: viewers call it AI slop, and foreign viewers don't buy. | **Skip it** until you have view velocity (about 150–200 engaged views per day per video). |
| **Direct CTAs** | Molly: three CTAs per video. | Trinder: CTAs should be gives, not takes; a hard CTA cost 30% of viewers. Kallaway: CTA after the second aha. | One **value CTA** (your Discord or a free guide) after a strong insight, then end on **another video**. |
| **A second channel** | Popular myth: Hormozi did it, so you should too. | Wes McDowell: only for a different audience or huge volume. Todd: align channels with audiences. | **One channel.** |

reads.title: What the strategists mean for Grow With Juliyan
reads.dek: The report's direct advice for your channel. Written in October, before the debloat video.
reads.md:
**The diagnosis.** Each upload gets fewer views (2.4K → 837 → 254). That fits the pattern every strategist describes: one outlier, then videos that dilute the signal. Your best video, "I Had 2 Hours to Glow Up Before a Date", has a **story, stakes and a time limit**. The worse ones are narrower experiments with less at stake ("dyed my eyebrows black"). Two uploads a month also means you get about 24 data points a year, which isn't enough to learn from.

**1. Write your channel hook sentence this week.** For example: "Welcome to Grow With Juliyan, the channel where I test what actually makes an average guy more attractive, with science, not looksmaxxing." Every video must fit it. Paddy's and Aprilynne's 80% rule is the test: would 80% of this video's viewers want your other videos?

**2. Pick one format for the next 10–15 videos.** You already have the right one: **"I tested / I tried X for N days"**. Vexian calls I built/I tried/I tested the personality trifecta, and Trakyo found "How I" videos earn 2–3x what "How to" videos earn. Make each one a story with an *intention and an obstacle*, stakes, a time limit and a head fake. "2 hours before a date" worked because it had all of these.

**3. Validate every idea before filming.** Search your topic and adjacent ones (men's style, skincare, fitness, nutrition, and for packaging *women's* beauty and self-improvement too) for outliers at 3x or more on channels under 100K subs from the last 6–12 months. Use the format-radar and competitor-dashboard tools you already have in this folder. No outlier pattern, no video.

**4. Use the unknown-mechanism framing.** It's tailor-made for science-based looks: "If you don't understand **sodium and cortisol**, you don't understand facial bloating." "Your face isn't fat, it's **water**." Put the mechanism in the content and the outcome in the title.

**5. Package on Kate Tolo's rules.** Lead with the most gossipy true fact. Follow every fear hook with a protocol. Speak simply, with visualisable numbers. Mock the thumbnail up beside competitors in a feed before you shoot. Plan the thumbnail *before* filming, with at least 3 different concepts and a real before/after or **mid-action** shot (Aprilynne). Keep thumbnail text to five words or fewer, and keep it different from the title.

**6. Intro checklist** (Colin & Samir plus Paddy): (1) show the thumbnail moment in the first second, (2) a hook line that isn't the title, (3) what the video is, (4) why *you* care (you're 18, you tried it on yourself; this is your Peter Parker positioning, not Batman), (5) a new loop, (6) a roadmap card. Keep it under 30–45 seconds. You already use wojak gags and one-second jokes; keep them only if the rest of the video stays that funny.

**7. Cadence.** For the next 12 weeks, **one long-form video a week** in the single format (Aprilynne's quantity arc). Then judge it on the 28-day picture, not on each upload. If that's impossible with school, do **at least 3 a month**. Two is too slow to learn from at 55 subs.

**8. Metrics to track per video.** Engaged views, the shape of the retention curve over the first 30 seconds, positive comments per 1,000 views, and subs per 1,000 views. Ignore the 1-of-10 ranking for 48 hours. Before each upload, write a prediction ("I expect 600 engaged views in 7 days because…") and compare.

**9. Your audience earns low CPMs.** Young male, international inventory pays little (Mac's numbers). Don't count on AdSense. Build towards affiliate and your own product, and keep growing the Discord: a community with rituals and a name (Primal Branding) is your real asset.

**10. Health-niche safety.** YouTube now demonetises AI "experts" on health topics. You're a real person showing real results, which is a moat, so stay evidence-based, cite sources on screen, and never fake a transformation. Make sure every thumbnail promise is actually delivered, or you lose hype eligibility.

**Things to stop doing.**
- Changing title or thumbnail within the first 48 hours without a reason.
- Narrow one-off experiments that don't belong to a series.
- Judging a format from a single video.
- Planning around a second channel, dubbing or video A/B tests.
- Starting thumbnails after the edit.

**A concrete 12-week plan.**
- **Week 1:** write the channel hook. Use the format radar to find 30 outliers across men's looks, fitness, skincare and women's glow-up. Extract 5 recurring formats and title psychologies.
- **Week 1:** brainstorm 50 ideas in the "I tested X" format, kill them down to 10 using Paddy's criteria, and write a one-page slide for each with a sketch, 10 titles and a logline.
- **Weeks 2–13:** one video a week. Thumbnail brief before the shoot. Use the intro checklist. One value CTA to the Discord. End on another video.
- **Every Sunday:** a post-mortem. What did I learn? Three things. Update the prediction log.
- **Week 7:** whichever topic or angle is your outlier, make **three more in a row** (Brent's double-down rule).
- **Week 13:** review. Go back to 2 a month at higher quality, or keep weekly if you have the momentum.

reads.title: Platform facts (autumn 2026)
reads.dek: Engaged views, the new YPP bar, and what YouTube shipped this season.
reads.md:
- **Views count from the first frame** for all formats (since 24–27 Aug 2026). The old metric is now called **engaged views**: about 10 seconds of hover-play, or any visit to the watch page. Revenue, CTR and the YPP Shorts path all use engaged views. Public counts often run 2–4x engaged views on big channels. Check the engaged-views column in Studio (Advanced mode).
- **YPP for new channels from Feb 2027:** **8,000 long-form public watch hours** (was 4,000) plus 1,000 subs, *or* 20M qualifying Shorts views. Shorts payouts need 10M views per rolling 90 days and are **decoupled** from long-form monetisation. You also need at least 3 public uploads. Live streams count towards watch hours.
- **Made on YouTube 2026:** video A/B tests with up to 3 cuts (selected creators from 2027, judged on watch time, cuts can't be too different). **Dynamic thumbnails** (3 thumbnails, each viewer sees the best one for them). Auto thumbnail swap and pre-publish feedback in Ask Studio. Analytics is renamed **Insights**, and the research tab now surfaces outliers (saved keywords are retired, so export them). **Ask YouTube** conversational search, which pulls clips from many creators. **Custom feeds.** Shorts series and seasons. **Shows** for YPP channels. Swappable sponsor segments, Amazon affiliate, AI comment moderation, conversational editing for Shorts, likeness detection, posts on TV, and 4K thumbnails (50MB).
- **Enforcement:** reach is reduced for channels that aggregate or re-upload others' clips. **AI "experts" on health or finance aren't eligible for monetisation.** Misleading or clickbait videos lose hype eligibility. Unsafe links, even spoken ones, can earn strikes. Realistic AI content must be disclosed. Re-uploading a removed video counts as circumvention and can terminate a channel.
- **TV:** YouTube has 14.2% of all US TV viewing against Netflix's 7.8%. TV viewers watch longer, so slower pacing and bigger text help there. *Your* audience is probably mostly on phones, so check the device split in Insights.
- **Subscribers matter less:** subs per view are trending down, and Todd says "the long-term trend has always been in that direction."

reads.title: What 544 hit and flop intros say
reads.dek: Your Intro Lab's rules for the first 30â€“60 seconds.
reads.md:
## How a good intro works
1. It delivers exactly what the title and thumbnail promised, in the first sentence. The best thumbnails show the result (a real before/after in the same light, a number, the finished look): 78% of videos with one were hits vs 32% without. It must be HIS result, not someone else's.
2. Sentence one is a promise or a surprising claim: the result he gets plus the cost ("…in 7 days, with stuff you already own"). Promise openings were hits 38 times vs 14 flops.
3. Make it cheap: minutes, $0, "realistic", "simple". A low price works the same way ("under $50" 3.9x, "under $700" 0.37x). An ease signal: 83% hits vs 41% without.
4. Within 15 s, name the cause or the stake: why it happens (salt, sleep, a myth) or what can go wrong.
5. Let him place himself: a question about his own face or body ("Is your face puffier in the morning than at night?"), a self-check ("signs you…") or a 10-second test he can do ("rub your forearm and smell it" was one video's most replayed moment).
6. By 30 s: the route on screen (numbered steps), one piece of SHOWN proof (a study on screen, same-light photos), and something planted for the end.
7. First concrete payoff by ~40 s, and make it the most visible, most wanted point.

## What kills intros
- Greeting, bio or channel name first (greeting openings: 17 hits vs 52 flops). Credentials only as proof after the promise.
- Series labels ("day 31", "episode 4", "welcome back to…"; every numbered episode in the lab flopped), sponsors or community plugs before the first payoff.
- Pure-feeling diagnosis ("if you feel stuck, watch this"), begging ("don't click off"), scolding the viewer.
- Overpromises and fake-precise numbers ("98.7% of women"); real numbers persuade.
- Copying a viral title or hook word for word: formulas burn out fast.
- Making it about my life instead of his result. Hedging ("hopefully", "kind of"), abstract words (mindset, journey).
Editing speed, talking speed, colour and showing my face did NOT decide anything.

My style: direct, personal, a bit funny; I use wojak memes (label the wojak as the viewer and show the change). Everything must be evidence-based and safe: no supplement hype, and "see a doctor" for anything medical. I speak about 3.5 words per second, so 30 seconds ≈ 105 words.

reads.title: What 542 full scripts say
reads.dek: Your Script Lab: what viewers replay, what they skip, and the point formula.
reads.md:
## What the data says
- Viewers navigate by section: the first seconds of a new section get 1.6x the replays of the seconds before it. Every section must open with its own hook (why he should care, what he'll get), not a label. Sections with hooks: 71% hits; without: 15%.
- Concrete steps win: when each point ends in an exact action (amount, time, product, schedule), 77% were hits vs 33%, and the body was watched as much as the intro.
- Most rewatched: a formula he can apply now, exact products/steps, a live demo, a vivid image, a surprising fact that changes what he'll do, the final reveal.
- Most skipped: theory before the action, my backstory, repetitive process footage, sponsor reads, outros. Theory blocks: 34% hits vs 59% without. Tangents: 19% vs 58%.
- Hold back the most wanted point AND say so ("the last one is the one most guys skip"): 74% hits vs 42%. Plant a deliverable for the end: the full routine on one screen got z9-z10 replay spikes; a measured winner revealed at the end got the lab's biggest (z17.9).
- Escalate: each section a step up from the last (85% hits vs 36%).
- End on value, not an outro: 87% hits vs 28%.
- Structures that held: routines and follow-alongs, systems with phases or a timeline (day 1 → day 7), full guides for one audience, self-checks ("signs you…"), rankings and countdowns, experiments with predictions and a measured result. Flopped: vlogs, Q&A, recorded talks, opinion rants.

## The point formula (repeat for every section)
1. Hook line: why this one matters or what he'll see.
2. The claim in one sentence.
3. The why in 20 seconds max, ideally with a study or number on screen.
4. Proof I can SHOW (photos, a measurement, me doing it).
5. The exact action: what, how much, how long, what it costs.
6. A bridge to the next point (the next question he has).

Order: intro → the most visible, most wanted point first → the other points → the planted payoff or verdict → one line of what to do now. Sponsors or self-promo only after the first payoff, and short. No "that's it for today" outro.

My channel: talking head plus wojak memes, evidence-based and safe (no supplement hype, "see a doctor" for anything medical). I speak about 3.5 words per second. Write plain spoken English, short sentences, more "you" than "I".

reads.title: What 4,135 titles and thumbnails say
reads.dek: Your Packaging Lab: each video compared with its own channel.
reads.md:
## Titles
- A specific qualifier in brackets did better in 8 of 13 channels: "(Full Guide)" (1.58x), "(Evidence-Based)", "(50% to 5%)". "Actually" did better in 6 of 8, an audience label ("for men", "teenagers") in 5 of 8, a colon or "|" in 5 of 7, a specific time or cost ("in 7 days", "under $50") in 6 of 10. Plain "how to" makes no difference either way.
- Did worse: money words (6 of 8 channels), "please watch this" / "watch this if" (4 of 4), emoji (4 of 4), and episode numbers ("Day 31": every one flopped).
- Formulas decay: "the top #" went from 1.41x to 0.74x as more people used it. Copy the structure, never the exact phrase.
- Real numbers beat fake-precise ones; believable beats huge.

## Thumbnails
- Show the outcome: a real before/after of me (same light, same angle, the after clearly better), the finished look, products I actually use, a number. Outcome thumbnails: 78% hits vs 32% without; someone else's transformation doesn't count, and a tired topic isn't saved by one.
- For product videos: lay every item out around my face with the price cap in 2-3 words ("UNDER $20"). Same layout, $50 vs $700: 3.9x vs 0.37x.
- One clear subject, high contrast, at most 4 words, readable at phone size. Text should add something the title doesn't say.
- More contrast and detail did better in most channels; very saturated, very colourful thumbnails didn't. A huge face close-up didn't help: what's shown matters more than the face.
- Avoid: only the "before", abstract concepts, logos or objects, someone else's face, spelling out the whole answer.
- Wojak thumbnails worked for a transformation (wojak → chad), not for opinions.

My brand: background #FFFEFB, blue #0571D3, red #F3080F, highlight #FF59F8, fonts Montserrat ExtraBold and Gloria Hallelujah. Everything must be honest and evidence-based: no promise the video doesn't keep.

reads.title: Gaps for a face creator
reads.dek: 105 English face channels, 2,339 videos: where demand is high and supply is low.
reads.md:
**Which channels count.** A channel is in if the same person appears inside most of its videos (face recognition on frames from inside 15 videos per channel, spread over the year) and its videos are spoken in English (YouTube's detected language on 2–3 videos per channel, plus the transcripts already fetched). Borderline channels I checked by eye on frame sheets. **105 channels and 2,339 scored videos pass** (33 core looks + 72 broader). Of the 226 niche channels, 96 failed the on-camera test and 55 failed the English test (32 failed both).

**The biggest change from the first report:** removing faceless and non-English channels empties out several "gaps". In the last 12 months, English face creators posted only **8 face-fat videos, 6 debloat videos and 11 facial-contrast videos**, and 18 eye-area videos. The demand for those topics was proven by faceless channels (34–39% hit rates in the full data). Among face creators they're almost unclaimed. That's either your biggest opening or a sign face creators avoid them. The data can't say which (**GUESS:** opening, because your before/after face is the thing faceless channels can't show).

### Top 5 gaps for a face creator

| # | Gap | Evidence (English face channels) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **"Am I still growing?" height guides for 17–21** | Height how-to: 56% of videos hit 2× (90% range 44–62%, n=27); 5-year hit rate 52% (n=44). Small-channel median 17.7K views. 16% of all questions under top height videos ask "can I still grow at my age?" **WEAK on spread:** only 5–6 channels post it. |
| 2 | **Jawline and mewing, practical and honest** | Jaw how-to: 44% hit (n=34, 10 channels), 5-year 50% (n=86). Mewing Q&A cluster 42% (n=24, 10 channels). Jaw has the most small channels with hits of any face topic (9). |
| 3 | **Hair care routine by hair type** | Hair how-to: 38.5% hit (n=26, 13 channels), 5-year 51% (n=225); 80% of the best videos are 2+ years old. 11% of hair-video questions are "what about my hair type?" |
| 4 | **The eye area** | 39% hit but only 18 videos in 12 months (**WEAK**); 5 years: 42% hit across 72 videos and 25 channels; median video 2.47× its channel, the highest of any face topic. |
| 5 | **Beard basics for young guys** | 46% hit (36–58%, n=55, 13 channels); 80% of the 5-year top 10 are 2+ years old. Only 1 small channel hit, so it rewards established channels. |

Plus the **"face in a faceless topic"** bet: debloat, face fat and contrast (details in Part 1).

### Top 10 packaging & editing rules for face creators (inside-channel comparisons)

1. **Your face, big, with 1–3 words.** Face in the thumbnail 1.24× (1.01–1.58), big face 1.13× (1.01–1.24), face-only 1.15×, 1–3 words 1.12× (1.04–1.21). No face 0.81×, no text 0.91×, scene 0.79×, screenshot 0.74×.
2. **Before/after stops mattering for face channels.** 0.98× automatic (0.88–1.09); 25% of winners vs 20% of medians by eye (p = 0.38). The before/after edge in the full data came from faceless channels.
3. **Name the audience:** "for men / as a guy" 1.69× (1.35–2.10), age/teen 1.28× (1.06–1.60).
4. **Tier lists:** 1.50× as an angle (1.23–1.83), 1.40× in titles.
5. **"How to"** 1.37× (1.17–1.66); how-to angle 1.25×.
6. **"I tried / I tested" works for face creators:** 1.28× (1.06–1.57, n=71). In the full data it was 1.15× and not distinguishable from 1.0.
7. **Don't frame it as a science explainer.** Explainer angle 0.84× (0.75–0.94); the word "explains" 0.55×. Teach the science inside a how-to or tier list instead.
8. **16–20 minutes:** 1.29× (1.14–1.50); under 5 minutes 0.59–0.67×.
9. **Open on the result, never a greeting.** Result-first openings: 15% of winners vs 5% of medians (p = 0.004). Greeting/intro first: 9% vs 22% (p = 0.005).
10. **One recurring title template, no episode numbers:** 1.47× (1.32–1.71).

**Editing intensity is not what separates face-channel winners.** Cuts per minute 5.9 vs 4.8 (p = 0.48), face on screen 80% vs 88% (p = 0.47). The "cut twice as often" rule from the first report doesn't hold inside face channels. The only near-signal: winners change what's on screen 7 times in the first minute vs 4 (p = 0.07, **WEAK**).

### Top 5 cross-niche formats (adjacent channels, all on camera)

| Format | Adjacent niches | Your niche (face, core) |
|---|---|---|
| One habit, N days, measured | 2.05× (1.63–2.47), 31 videos, 6 ch | 4 videos (0.15%) |
| Science reacts to TikTok / Reddit / headlines | 2.25× (1.71–5.26), 35 videos, 4 ch | 0 |
| Cheap vs expensive / every price point | 1.48× (1.34–1.72), 61 videos, 9 ch | 2 videos |
| Products that steal your money | 1.67× (1.13–2.46), 38 videos, 12 ch | 6 videos |
| I tried someone else's routine | 1.83× (1.25–2.47), 18 videos, 3 ch, **WEAK** | 1 video |

reads.title: How to read a book so it sticks
reads.dek: Your note-taking system: from margin marks to a video idea or a habit.
reads.md:
The goal is that **every book ends up as entries in notes you already reread**. Nothing gets saved just to be saved.

**1. While reading (0 extra minutes).** Pencil only, in the margin: `|` = idea, `★` = steal this, `?` = I doubt this. Don't write notes mid-session. Reading time is for reading.

**2. Last 5 min of each session (this is the §4 rule).** Close the book. In Notes, write **3 ideas from memory, in your own words**. Active recall is what makes it stick (`LRN01` A). Under each idea, write one line, **"So for me:"**, and give it **one route**:

| Tag | Goes to | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **V**: video idea | Ideas list, written as a **working title** (you work title-first) | Burn → "Why the gym won't make you lean (the Hadza study)" |
| **H**: habit | "Habit candidates" list. It only gets used at the Sunday review, **one rollout change at a time** | Storyworthy → Homework for Life, 5 min at 22:55 |
| **R**: rule | Your how-to-youtube rules note (reread every Sunday) | Zinsser → "Final script pass: cut 10% of words" |
| **F**: niche fact | Niche facts note, **with book + page** so you can cite it on camera | Etcoff → the averageness/symmetry findings |
| **X**: nothing | Fine. Not every idea needs a route | |

**3. Within 48 h of finishing (your 48-hour test).** Write a **book card** of 10 lines or fewer:
- The 3 ideas I read it for (from memory first, then check the margins).
- The 1 thing I'll change, and when.
- 3 video titles it gave me.
- One `?` I still doubt, and why.
- Verdict: reread / done / I should have read a summary.

**4. Spaced review (2 min, Sunday review step 5).** Pick one old book card, cover it, and recall the 3 ideas. If you can't, the idea didn't stick. Reread only that section.

**5. Kill rules.**
- After 2 sessions (about 50 pages) with zero V/H/R/F routes, drop the book and write "X" on its card.
- If a whole book produced zero routes, stop reading books *like it* and use summaries for that kind instead.

**Bonus:** Storyworthy's Homework for Life *is* a note method. Use one line a day at the 22:55 tracker for "the most story-worthy moment today". After a month you'll have about 30 personal openers for videos.
